label: Run 14 · Ali Wong
note: Written by Ali Wong from what they wrote about the two characters, improvisation by improvisation (run 14: run 13 told as improvisation instructions, without the game's language; traps two long). Before each of the 11 improvisations the writer was told how it goes for Reuben_404: the approach taken, how well it comes off, how it goes wrong on a miss, any trap (a way of going wrong that carries on into the next improvisations: Spiral, Overthinking, Fixation and the rest) and how the other's interest moves. IMPROVISATIONS holds each instruction and what the writer wrote for it. The instructions are part of the design and stay. Score the chat as the reader gets it, the bar unchanged, but read each part against what was asked: where a score comes from what an instruction asked for (a fumble, a trap, interest lost or won), its cause is the improvisation; where the writer carried an instruction out badly, or the weakness has nothing to do with the instructions, it is the writing. The reader sees no dice and no plan: where a dimension speaks of turns, read improvisations.

chat.test.why: For Reuben the reader gets all four, and they are linked: the fear of vanishing, the bit and the denials, Delphine and the pity voice, and dropping the act at the end. The fear arrives because he says it outright in Improvisation 5 (a Self-awareness/Dread catastrophe), so it is half-stated rather than discovered. For Brick the reader gets the habit, the origin (cab, Marguerite) and the end. Her fear is only reached through her own stated maxim, and the reader says outright that the chat 'never states this as a fear'. It stays above the line because both endings follow from the fears: Brick's 'recurring indefinitely' answers 'sometime means never', and Reuben's 'no fake voice' answers the vanishing. It misses 5 because both fears come out by statement and Brick's childhood detail connects to nothing.
evidence: if i stop tap-dancing for 10 seconds i'll vanish
"Sometime" means never.
Calendar invite sent, recurring indefinitely.
chat.test.raise: Let Brick's fear surface in a slip, such as her flinching at an open-ended phrase of his, rather than in her own explanation, and tie the pigs-in-a-blanket childhood to the need for control.

chat.sideways.why: Improvisation 3's Denial does real sideways work: the freezing flat, the ring light and the pity voice all come out as Reuben being caught, which gives the origin of one habit by slip. Almost everything else is stated or volunteered. Brick's origin is given on request with 'I'm militant because', Marguerite is volunteered unprompted in Improvisation 4, and Delphine and the mirror rehearsal are confessed outright. The boxed rosé is asked for and handed over with 'Fine'. Because most of the important facts are stated, it sits below the line.

chat.subtext.why: There are places where the avoidance is legible: the denials in Improvisations 3 and 7, 'don't tease me with logistics unless you mean it', and the boxed rosé drunk standing up. Feelings are also named or explained many times, though. Reuben has 'i'll vanish', 'so you wouldn't laugh at my body first', 'publicly imploding' and 'trauma-dumping', and Brick has 'left me sobbing in a cab'. The two Self-awareness/Dread catastrophes (Improvisations 5 and 8) asked for narration, but the writer turned it into therapy-style explanation, and Brick's explanations are not asked for by any instruction.

It falls short of a 6 because several calls also leaned on content: #2 on the "4.5-inch left hook", #11 on Marguerite, #13 on the top hat. But Improvisations 5 and 8 have him narrate his own act ("oh god i'm doing the bit again"), which is a character pointing out his own gap. Brick has almost no gap. chat.escalation.why: The 12-minute clock, the denials and the Marguerite/Delphine reveals keep things moving, and the night is not settled early: Tuesday is offered around message 10 and not accepted until the end. But the shape is set by "'Sometime' means never". From "Bold recovery at the buzzer" (Improvisation 9) onward, the probe reader stops and calls every beat, and Improvisations 10–11 are a four-message victory lap. The writing also blunts the clock: "23:42 on the dot" arrives after Reuben has already claimed "30 seconds" and sent a full itinerary, so the deadline never bites, and the date drifts between Tuesday 20:00 and 23:58.

chat.wince.why: The reader almost never knows something a character doesn't before it goes off. Improvisations 5 and 8 asked for Dread, failure narrated as it happens, so those dangers are announced as they land ("watching my thumb ruin this in real time"). The nearest setup is "Let's audit the boomerang", which tips us that his act will crack, but nothing precise is planted to go off on the wrong spot. The second denial is pre-telegraphed only by repeating the pattern.

Her contempt for "Mirror-rehearsed spontaneity" is quietly contradicted by her own scripted opening inventory, but the chat never makes that land, and the ending mostly vindicates her. chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest break is Reuben's:

"oh god i'm doing the bit again. this is why Delphine walked out, i can't say one un-performed sentence because if i stop tap-dancing for 10 seconds i'll vanish"

You can tell because he steps outside the routine and names it. Before this, his confessions come as jokes or inverted denials ("i definitely haven't been in a freezing flat for 11 days..."), so the truth is smuggled in while the bit keeps running. Here there's no denial and no punchline. He says outright that he performs, why he does it, and what it has cost him (Delphine). The next line, about sweating under the top hat and watching his thumb "ruin this in real time," keeps that same unguarded tone.

Brick_haus has a matching moment:

"Fine. It's a three-liter box and I'm drinking it standing up because I threw out every chair Marguerite ever touched."

"Fine" marks a concession. She takes back her own earlier claim of "estate rosé" and gives up the polished, clock-auditing persona to admit something unflattering about her life since Marguerite. It's the only time she contradicts herself, and she does it because he asked.

Reuben's later line, "i'm dropping the act, bringing two chairs and pigs-in-a-blanket," says it's the drop, but it's less clean. It immediately turns back into a timestamped itinerary, the same playful format they've been using all along. Still, it's built from the things the two of them admitted earlier (her missing chairs, her childhood food), which suggests the earlier admissions were real.

One limit: the whole exchange is stylized, and even the "sincere" lines still contain jokes ("wet cashew"). From the text alone I can only point to where the register shifts. I can't confirm that either person actually meant it.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

**What he's afraid of.** He fears that without a performance there is nothing of him left: "if i stop tap-dancing for 10 seconds i'll vanish." He also fears being laughed at for his body: "i practiced my 'casual' opener in the mirror so you wouldn't laugh at my body first." And he fears being pitied. He brings this up through a denial: "nobody has EVER said 'we can just watch something' in a pity voice when my curve caught wrong, okay?"

**What he does so he doesn't have to feel it.** He does "the bit," meaning constant jokes and a put-on persona ("i can't say one un-performed sentence," "my fake voice"). He also denies things in a way that gives them away: "i definitely haven't been in a freezing flat for 11 days clamping a ring light to my headboard to hide my crooked shadow. i'm out EVERY night." He presents himself as carefree and uncommitted: "i don't do calendars baby, i just drift from party to party like a bent boomerang." Brick calls this out: "blocking anyone who says 'drift' when he clearly replied in four seconds."

**Where it comes from.** The chat ties it to Delphine leaving: "this is why Delphine walked out." The pity-voice moment is implied to have happened, given how he denies it. Anything earlier, such as childhood or why the performing started, is not in the chat.

**What he did at the end.** He dropped the act and committed in concrete terms: "i'm dropping the act, bringing two chairs and pigs-in-a-blanket, and letting you schedule my left hook down to the second." He followed with "no ring light, no fake bands… 08:00: i'm still there" and "every week after—no fake voice."

**Brick_haus**

**What they're afraid of.** The chat never states this as a fear outright. The closest is the fear of vague promises that mean being left: "'Sometime' means never."

**What they do so they don't have to feel it.** They run a strict clock with deadlines and threats. "you have until 23:42 to earn a calendar invite," "Sixty seconds until I archive you. Make a choice," "Stop lying or you lose the slot." They also stay cool and cutting rather than soft: "Deeply embarrassing spiral, Reuben… Pull your foreskin together." Whether the scheduling is protection is my reading. They describe it as a reason ("I'm militant because…"), not as a defence.

**Where it comes from.** Two past events are cited. The first: "the last dick who said 'let's do this again sometime' without naming a day left me sobbing in a cab." The second: "My ex Marguerite dumped me for scheduling our fights with hard end-times." So the same habit also cost them a relationship. They also say they "threw out every chair Marguerite ever touched" and mention "the microwave pigs-in-a-blanket I grew up on." How the childhood detail connects to the fear is not in the chat.

**What they did at the end.** They accepted Reuben and committed in their own terms: "Calendar invite sent, recurring indefinitely." Just before that, they admitted the specifics had moved them: "That itinerary just made my ridge bump throb." Whether they let the deadline slide is unclear, because the timestamps don't line up. Reuben says 23:41 and then "30 seconds before i blow this forever," and Brick then says "23:42 on the dot."

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
**Where I'd have stopped**

I'd have stopped after "Bold recovery at the buzzer. Send me the exact itinerary right now and I might not block you." At that point the 12-minute deadline, the real engine of the chat, has been resolved. Reuben dropped the act, Brick signalled acceptance, and the stakes are gone. The four messages after that are a victory lap: the itinerary, Brick's "ridge bump throb," Reuben's promise of "every week after," and the recurring invite. The closing landlord/security-deposit callback is a good button, but I wouldn't have stayed for it.

A weaker drop-off point comes earlier, in the Marguerite-then-Delphine stretch. Brick reveals an ex who left over scheduling, and in the very next message Reuben reveals an ex who left over his performing. That symmetry feels templated rather than discovered. "Deeply embarrassing spiral" and the clock countdown pull the chat back, which is the only reason I'd keep going there.

**Where the next beat was exactly predictable**

- **"Sometime means never."** Once Brick names the deadline, a past hurt, and contempt for vague promises, while Reuben keeps issuing transparent denials, the rom-com shape is set. He will drop the act at the last second with a concrete, scheduled offer, and she'll accept. I didn't know the details, but I knew the outcome.
- **"I definitely do NOT want you to hold me down…"** By the third "i definitely haven't / nobody has EVER / i definitely do NOT," the denial pattern is fully established. Brick's "Transparent denial at 23:40" is the expected reply.
- **"Sixty seconds until I archive you. Make a choice."** From here it's fully predictable that Reuben makes the sincere pitch and wins. His callback to the chairs and pigs-in-a-blanket is neat, but it's exactly the kind of callback you'd expect.
- **"Bold recovery at the buzzer."** Both the itinerary and the acceptance were certain from this point.

**Things that snagged on a read-through**

The text doesn't explain these, so I'm only noting them:

- **The deadline.** It's 23:42, but Brick says "23:42 on the dot" only after Reuben has already passed the "30 seconds" mark and sent a full itinerary. The deadline neither bites nor gets extended; the chat just slides past it.
- **The date.** Reuben first proposes "Tuesday, 20:00." The final itinerary starts "23:58: i show up," which reads like tonight, and his last message says "23:58, Tuesday." It's unclear whether this is tonight, Tuesday at 20:00, or Tuesday at 23:58.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
I think it ends with Brick saying yes, probably by actually sending the calendar invite right at 23:42, in a dry, clipped line that sounds like a reprimand but works as an acceptance. My guess is she confirms Reuben's Tuesday 20:00 slot, maybe tightens his schedule or adds a stipulation about the chairs, and leaves it there.

Here's why I read it that way.

**The deadline is built to be beaten.** Brick sets the 23:42 cutoff in her first line and counts it down almost every turn after: four minutes, three minutes, 23:40, sixty seconds. A countdown like that usually exists so someone can make it with seconds to spare, and Reuben lands his last message "30 seconds before i blow this."

**His final message meets each of her stated conditions:**
- **"Make a choice."** He does, explicitly.
- **"Stop lying or you lose the slot."** He announces he's "dropping the act."
- **"Sometime" means never.** He has already named a day and time, Tuesday at 20:00, the one thing her ex in the cab never did.

**His offer is a set of callbacks to what she let slip:**
- **Two chairs** answer her admission that she threw out every chair Marguerite touched and drinks standing up.
- **Pigs-in-a-blanket** answer her confession about the microwave version she grew up on.
- **Letting her schedule him "down to the second"** answers the Marguerite story, where her scheduling was the reason she was left. He's offering to welcome the trait that cost her.

**Both have already broken character.** Reuben's spiral about Delphine and Brick's boxed-wine confession show both personas cracking. The scene seems to be about two over-performers getting to a sincere moment, and his last line is that moment.

What could make me wrong: Brick's voice is consistently tart, so the ending could be a fake-out, like "archived" followed by a reversal, or her grading his answer before accepting. Reuben could also slip back into a bit and get punished for it. The text doesn't rule those out. But everything it sets up points toward her accepting, and I'd expect her to do it in her own terse, scheduling-obsessed way rather than warmly.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
These are the callbacks I can find, with how each one shifts when it returns.

**Victorian landlords and the security deposit.** Reuben opens by joking that they look like two landlords about to cheat someone out of a deposit, which makes them partners against a third party. In Brick's last line he is still the "landlord," but now he is the one "forfeiting your entire security deposit on my ridge bump." The deposit has become something he surrenders to her rather than something they take from someone else. It reads as both sexual and as him committing.

**The top hat.** At first it's just costume. Later he is "sweating under a top hat that cost more than my rent," so it becomes a sign of the expensive performance he's straining to keep up. At the end Brick says "keep the top hat on," which takes the prop back as something she likes, now that the act is dropped.

**The clock and the 23:42 deadline.** The schedule "tattooed down your shaft" starts as a flirtatious detail. It becomes a test with a countdown ("four minutes," "three minutes," "sixty seconds until I archive you") and then a threat. Brick's "23:42 on the dot" lands as the moment he passes. The timestamped itinerary also changes from a joke ("20:04: you audit my… bank charge") to a sincere offer ("08:00: i'm still there").

**The calendar invite.** Brick says he has until 23:42 to "earn a calendar invite," and Reuben answers "i don't do calendars." At the end she sends one, "recurring indefinitely." It changes from a hurdle into commitment, and Reuben's stance on it fully reverses.

**"Sometime" and naming a day.** Brick says "sometime" means never. Reuben answers with "Tuesday," and Tuesday comes back in his final pledge with "every week after." The specific day becomes the proof of sincerity. The time changes between mentions, from 20:00 to 23:58, and the chat doesn't explain why.

**Hard end-times and Marguerite.** Brick's ex left her for scheduling fights with hard end-times. Brick still runs everything on a strict clock, but the final invite has no end. Her habit of setting end-times, which cost her that relationship, turns into an open-ended commitment.

**The left hook (his curve).** At first it's a jaunty disclosure that feels "weirdly safe," and then a carabiner joke. It darkens with the "crooked shadow" and the curve that "caught wrong," which point to shame. Later he offers to let her "schedule my left hook," and finally it's "my crooked hook keeping you company." The same body part moves from joke to insecurity to something he offers up and that is accepted.

**The ridge bump.** It starts as Brick's matching disclosure and then the other half of the carabiner joke. It returns as arousal ("made my ridge bump throb") and finally as the place he forfeits his deposit. The meaning moves from a fair-trade confession to desire.

**Drift and the boomerang.** Reuben claims he drifts "like a bent boomerang." Brick threatens to block anyone who says "drift" and says "let's audit the boomerang." The bend in the image also echoes his curve. The word itself doesn't come back after that.

**Audit.** "Audit the boomerang" is skeptical scrutiny. In Reuben's itinerary, "you audit my… girth-pump bank charge" turns it into invited, kinky exposure. By "one final audit" and "audit away," it is welcome.

**The ring light and the freezing flat.** He denies spending 11 days in a freezing flat with a ring light hiding his shadow. Later he promises to "show up shivering, no ring light." What he hid becomes what he openly brings. He also says "no fake bands," but nothing earlier in the chat mentions bands, so I can't tell what that refers to.

**Being held down so he can't talk.** "You pin me down until i shut up" starts as part of the jokey schedule. It comes back as a denial that is really a wish ("i definitely do NOT want you to hold me down… so i can't do my fake voice"). It ends as a plain request: "sit on my chest so i can't speak." The joke turns into a sincere wish to be stopped from performing.

**The fake voice, the act, and performing.** "I can't say one un-performed sentence" and the mirror-rehearsed opener lead to "dropping the act" and "no fake voice." The idea moves from a confession of the problem to a promise to stop.

**The denial pattern.** He keeps saying "I definitely haven't," "nobody has EVER," "I definitely do NOT." Brick names it as "oddly specific denial," then "transparent denial." The first denials hide sad truths, while the last one hides desire.

**The box rosé.** Brick's "estate rosé" comes back when Reuben asks whether it's really boxed, and she admits it's a three-liter box. Her pretension gets deflated the same way his has been, and she makes a confession of her own.

**Pigs-in-a-blanket.** They first appear in Brick's memory of the food she grew up on. Reuben then offers to bring them, turning her vulnerable detail into a gift.

**The chairs and the empty floor.** Brick threw out every chair Marguerite touched, which is why she drinks standing. Reuben's "that empty floor" picks this up, and then he promises to bring two chairs. Her loss becomes something he offers to repair.

**Blocking and archiving.** Brick's threats to block, archive, or make him "lose the slot" recur and soften to "I might not block you" before the invite is sent. The threat holds steady until it's withdrawn.

**Exes.** Delphine is mentioned once and doesn't come back. Marguerite comes back through the chairs, and through the end-times point above.
